questions.learningObjective: Explain non-chord tone classification
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain why a passing tone is classified as a non-chord tone even when it sounds consonant.

answer.exemplar: A passing tone is defined by its melodic function between two chord tones, not by consonance; if it is not a member of the sounding chord, it remains a non-chord tone.

questions.explanation: Chord membership depends on the chord's pitch classes, not on consonance. A passing tone moves between chord tones but is not one of them.
questions.hint: Membership, not consonance, defines chord tones.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Bass motion across an authentic cadence
questions.learningObjective: Explain authentic cadence bass
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain why the bass descends from five to one in an authentic cadence.

answer.exemplar: The bass moves from dominant to tonic, creating the strongest harmonic closure; the descending motion by four scale steps reinforces the sense of arrival at the tonic.

questions.explanation: Dominant to tonic is the strongest progression. The bass descent from five to one marks that arrival clearly.
questions.hint: Dominant to tonic gives closure.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The members of a triad
questions.learningObjective: Identify triad members in minor
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, a table lists D, F, A; what triad is this?

options.text: D major, root D with major third and perfect fifth
D minor, root D with minor third and perfect fifth
D diminished, root D with minor third and diminished fifth
D augmented, root D with major third and augmented fifth

questions.explanation: D, F, A is a minor triad: root D, minor third F, perfect fifth A. The other options alter the third or fifth.
questions.hint: Check the third's size.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The interval from a first-inversion bass to the root
questions.learningObjective: Compare first-inversion intervals
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, which interval from first-inversion bass to root is larger than the chord's third?

options.text: A fourth, because the inversion flips the interval
A third, because the bass is the third
A sixth, because the bass-to-root span exceeds the third
An octave, because the root repeats

questions.explanation: The interval from first-inversion bass to root is a sixth, larger than the third that defines the bass. The other options misstate the span.
questions.hint: First inversion gives a sixth.

questions.topic: Root position against first inversion
questions.learningObjective: Explain root position stability
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain why root position is considered the most stable chord position.

answer.exemplar: Root position places the root in the bass, aligning the lowest voice with the chord's fundamental; this alignment gives the strongest sense of tonal grounding and stability.

questions.explanation: The root in the bass aligns the lowest note with the chord's foundation. That alignment produces the most stable sonority.
questions.hint: Root in bass equals foundation.

questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, a major seventh chord spans how many semitones from root to seventh?
questions.explanation: A major seventh is eleven semitones above the root. That span defines the major seventh chord's top interval.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The interval from a second-inversion bass to the root
questions.learningObjective: Explain second-inversion interval
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain why the interval from a second-inversion bass to the root is a fourth.

answer.exemplar: In second inversion the bass is the fifth, and the fifth sits a fourth below the root; measuring upward from that bass to the root therefore spans four scale steps.

questions.explanation: The bass is the fifth, which lies a fourth below the root. Measuring upward gives a fourth.
questions.hint: Fifth to root is a fourth.

questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, how many leading tones does a major scale contain?
questions.explanation: A major scale has one leading tone, scale degree seven. Only that degree sits a semitone below tonic.

questions.topic: Counting the tones a change of key holds in common
questions.learningObjective: Compare common-tone counts
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, which pair of keys shares more tones: C major and G major, or C major and F major?

options.text: Neither shares any tones, because keys are disjoint
C and G share more, because G has two sharps
C and F share more, because F has two flats
Both share six tones, because each differs by one accidental

questions.explanation: Both G major and F major differ from C major by a single accidental, so each shares six pitch classes. The counts are equal.
questions.hint: Each has one accidental difference.

questions.topic: Borrowed chords in a major key
questions.learningObjective: Identify borrowed chord quality
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, in C major which borrowed chord has a flat sixth scale degree in its root?

options.text: VI, A major, because it is diatonic to C major
bVI, Ab major, because it borrows the sixth degree from C minor
iv, F minor, because it borrows the fourth degree
options.misconception: confuses degree six with degree four

options.text: bIII, Eb major, because it borrows the third degree
options.misconception: confuses degree six with degree three

questions.explanation: bVI is Ab major, built on the lowered sixth degree borrowed from C minor. The other options select different degrees or diatonic chords.
questions.hint: Lowered sixth degree gives bVI.

questions.learningObjective: List bass members for seventh positions
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, list the bass member for each of the four positions of a seventh chord.

answer.exemplar: Root position has the root in the bass, first inversion the third, second inversion the fifth, and third inversion the seventh; each position is named by its lowest pitch.

questions.explanation: Each inversion is named by the chord member in the bass. The seventh in the bass gives the last inversion.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The tritone inside a dominant seventh
questions.learningObjective: Resolve tritone by contrary motion
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain how the tritone in a dominant seventh resolves to tonic.

answer.exemplar: The tritone's two notes move by semitone in opposite directions: the lower note rises and the upper note falls, landing on the tonic's root and third.

questions.explanation: Contrary motion by semitone resolves the tritone's tension. The lower note rises and the upper note falls to stable tonic tones.
questions.hint: Opposite semitone motion.

questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, what distinguishes a triad from a seventh chord?

A triad has four pitch classes, a seventh chord has three
A triad has three pitch classes, a seventh chord has four
A triad needs a root, a seventh chord does not

questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain how a function table helps test whether a chord root fits a given harmonic function.

answer.exemplar: A function table maps each scale degree to its harmonic function, so comparing a chord's root to the table reveals whether that root supports tonic, pre-dominant, or dominant function.

questions.explanation: The table links scale degrees to functions. Matching the root to its degree tests its function directly.

questions.topic: Locating the pivot chord in a modulation
questions.learningObjective: Explain locating a pivot chord
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, explain how to locate the pivot chord when a passage modulates.

answer.exemplar: Find the chord that belongs to both the old and new keys, then mark where the harmony begins to favor the new key; that shared chord is the pivot.

questions.explanation: The pivot is the shared chord. Locating it requires checking membership in both keys and the point of tonal reorientation.
questions.hint: Shared membership plus reorientation point.
